summary: Intermittent 429s after scheduled clock skew + mixed batch/stream traffic — unclear refill semantics
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports recurring 429 responses across mixed batch-embedding ingestion and low-latency chat streams. Pattern appears after a scheduled clock skew correction in the customer environment (they run cluster time sync every night). The 429s start ~30s after the time correction and persist for several minutes in bursts.

Impact:
- Customer ingestion pipeline (bulk embeddings) sees ~10% of requests rejected with 429s for 3-8 minutes during the window.
- Interactive chat to support agents experiences sporadic short-lived 429s causing degraded UX.

Environment:
- NovaHealth production (enterprise plan) in us-west region
- Traffic mix: background batched embedding workers (50 qps bursts) + interactive websocket streams (20 concurrent)

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Ensure server nodes run ntp-sync job (simulate a 5s forward time jump).
2) Start a bulk-embed job with 100 concurrent short requests and a few persistent websocket chat sessions.
3) Observe 429s appearing roughly 20-40 seconds after the clock adjustment.

Observed behavior:
- 429s include X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0 and Retry-After headers of small values (3-10s), but retries still result in 429s until the spike clears.
- Console shows token buckets refilling less predictably; tenant-level counters appear to be out of sync briefly.

Expected behavior:
- Rate limiter should be robust to small clock adjustments; refill math shouldn't cause a token deficit across mixed connection types.

Attachments:
- Customer logs (session IDs provided) and a pcap of one websocket session uploaded to the ticket.
comments: 2026-02-20 - Avery Chen: Opened ticket after CS call with NovaHealth. They provided logs and a timeline correlating 429 bursts with nightly ntp run.
2026-02-20 - Diego Marquez: Assigned for SRE investigation. Asking for exact ntp offset observed and exact API keys used in sample traces.
2026-02-20 - NovaHealth (customer): Provided offsets: two nodes jumped +4s and +6s respectively. Uploaded request traces and sample bulk job id 'embed-20260220-81a'.

2026-02-21 - Diego Marquez: Initial hypothesis: refill schedule uses wall-clock windows that can 'skip' a refill when time moves forward, causing temporary negative bucket balance for short-lived streams that don't re-request refill immediately.
2026-02-21 - Support (Sana Patel): Requested a temporary mitigation: recommend staggering the customer's ntp job or configuring a short exponential backoff on retries while we investigate.
investigation_notes: Pulled rate-limiter metrics for tenant NovaHealth between 02:00-02:10 UTC on 2026-02-20. Observed sawtooth drops in token count coinciding with ntp sync at 02:03:12 UTC.

Token refill is implemented with an epoch-aligned refill tick (1s granularity). A forward clock jump causes the refill loop to compute a larger-than-expected delta and then cap it, but internal accounting path for websocket-anchored sessions uses last-seen-timestamp which briefly lags, leading to double-debiting of pending requests.

Found one race: pre-counting logic for multipart bulk uploads increments an in-flight counter, then the refill path subtracts tokens based on elapsed time. If elapsed time jumps forward, accounting runs a fast-path that resets refill timers but doesn't reconcile the in-flight counter until after the request processing completes — leading to momentary negative effective quota.
Reproduced locally by forcing process clock jump in an integration harness. Confirmed 429s appear for mixed websocket + REST burst traffic when refill tick and websocket last-seen timestamps diverge.
Related systems: edge-proxy keeps per-connection state; if connections experience different system times (e.g., different hosts in a pooled IP set), aggregated tenant accounting can be skewed.
Metrics examined: tenant_token_balance, refill_tick_latency, per-route_inflight_count. Refill_tick_latency spiked during time jump.
resolution: Mitigation provided (2026-02-21): Recommended short-term customer workarounds: 1) Stagger NTP sync across hosts so not all nodes jump simultaneously; 2) Enable client-side jittered retry/backoff for bulk workers (recommended policy: initial_retry=250ms, backoff=1.5x, max=8s); 3) Temporarily isolate high-throughput batch worker keys into their own route to avoid competing with low-latency websockets.

Engineering fix (tracked): Implement a reconciliation pass in the rate-limiter to clamp negative effective balances when a forward clock jump is detected and to reconcile per-connection last-seen timestamps with tenant-level refill timestamps on the next refill tick. Patch proposed in PR #2241 and integration tests added to cover clock shifts.
Rollout notes: Patch will be staged to canary on 2026-02-24, monitored for refill_tick_latency regressions. If stable, promote to us-west prod by 2026-02-26 during a low-traffic window.
Postmortem follow-up: Add runbook guidance about scheduled time-syncs for enterprise customers and a console warning when refill_latency exceeds 500ms.
notes_for_followup: Confirm with NovaHealth after canary that 429s no longer correlate with nightly ntp job.
Add e2e scenario to customer onboarding docs explaining how to test for quota stability during node time resyncs.
Evaluate long-term: consider shifting refill to monotonic-clock based deltas to avoid wall-clock anomalies.
